title: When cGMP Rises: Arteries and Drugs

scenes.visual: Dark slate (#0F172A) frame, reusing the first film's colour map. A cross-section of an artery wall fills 70% of the frame height: a single layer of endothelial cells lining the lumen at top, and a tense vascular smooth muscle cell beneath holding emerald-green (#34D399) soluble guanylyl cyclase, a low teal (#2DD4BF) cGMP gauge, and rose (#F43F5E) PDE5. Off-white title 'When cGMP Rises: Arteries and Drugs' (size 40) fades in and cleanly fades out by 2.0 s.

scenes.tts: In the first film, a rod reported light by driving c G M P down from baseline. Why does that exact same molecule rise to relax an artery, and how do drugs alter it? A classic vessel experiment pointed the way.
scenes.caption: In the first film, a rod reported light by driving cGMP down from baseline. Why does that exact same molecule rise to relax an artery, and how do drugs alter it? A classic vessel experiment pointed the way.
scenes.visual: Hold the artery-wall cross-section while a brief left-hand inset echoes the first film's dropping teal (#2DD4BF) rod gauge, then dissolves so the artery wall fills the frame. Inside the smooth muscle cell, the teal cGMP gauge sits low and contractile filaments appear taut and shortened.
scenes.narration: In the first film, a rod reported light by driving cGMP down from baseline. Why does that exact same molecule rise to relax an artery, and how do drugs alter it? A classic vessel experiment pointed the way.

scenes.tts: Mount a ring of rabbit artery in warm oxygenated salt solution and add acetylcholine. When the thin inner lining, the endothelium, stays intact, the artery ring relaxes and widens. Rub that lining off, and acetylcholine no longer relaxes the ring. The lining must pass a signal to the muscle beneath.

scenes.visual: Morph the artery cross-section smoothly into two paired schematic artery rings side by side (labelled 'Intact lining' and 'Lining removed', schematic): gold (#FACC15) acetylcholine dots wash over both. The intact ring expands cleanly while the rubbed ring stays tight and narrow. A gentle arrow points from the intact endothelial lining downward into the smooth muscle ring.

scenes.tts: On an endothelial cell, acetylcholine binds its receptor and raises its calcium. Calcium switches on nitric oxide synthase, which makes nitric oxide gas from arginine. Small and uncharged, this gas needs no vesicles or channels. It diffuses freely across both membranes and reacts away within seconds, reaching only near neighbors.
scenes.caption: On an endothelial cell, acetylcholine binds its receptor and raises its calcium. Calcium switches on nitric oxide synthase, which makes nitric oxide gas from arginine. scenes.visual: Return smoothly to the full-frame artery-wall cross-section. Gold acetylcholine binds a receptor on the top endothelial cell; coral-orange (#FB923C) calcium dots rise and dock onto a block labelled 'NO synthase'. Glowing violet (#C084FC) nitric oxide dots emerge, drift straight across both cell membranes into the smooth muscle cell below, and fade away quickly if they drift farther.
scenes.narration: On an endothelial cell, acetylcholine binds its receptor and raises its calcium. Calcium switches on nitric oxide synthase, which makes nitric oxide gas from arginine. Small and uncharged, this gas needs no vesicles or channels. It diffuses freely across both membranes and reacts away within seconds, reaching only near neighbors.

scenes.tts: In smooth muscle, nitric oxide binds the heme iron of soluble guanylyl cyclase. The enzyme switches on, and c G M P climbs sharply. That rise activates protein kinase G, which works against contraction. The muscle relaxes, and the artery widens.
scenes.caption: In smooth muscle, nitric oxide binds the heme iron of soluble guanylyl cyclase. The enzyme switches on, and cGMP climbs sharply. That rise activates protein kinase G, which works against contraction. The muscle relaxes, and the artery widens.
scenes.visual: Violet (#C084FC) nitric oxide dots bind a small glowing heme pocket on emerald-green (#34D399) soluble guanylyl cyclase. Teal (#2DD4BF) cGMP dots stream outward and drive the teal gauge sharply upward. Teal cGMP switches on a block labelled 'PKG', the smooth muscle's contractile filaments lengthen smoothly, and the lumen above widens. Rose (#F43F5E) PDE5 sits in the corner, dimmed and unlabelled for now.
scenes.narration: In smooth muscle, nitric oxide binds the heme iron of soluble guanylyl cyclase. The enzyme switches on, and cGMP climbs sharply. That rise activates protein kinase G, which works against contraction. The muscle relaxes, and the artery widens.

scenes.caption: But nitric oxide does not last. Once it stops arriving, the cyclase falls quiet. Think back to the rod, where an enzyme destroyed this same messenger. What could bring cGMP back down, so the muscle tightens again?
scenes.tts: But nitric oxide does not last. Once it stops arriving, the cyclase falls quiet. Think back to the rod, where an enzyme destroyed this same messenger. What could bring c G M P back down, so the muscle tightens again?
scenes.visual: The violet nitric oxide dots fade away and emerald-green soluble guanylyl cyclase dims. The teal (#2DD4BF) cGMP gauge holds high. A small faded inset of the first film's rod, with its rose (#F43F5E) PDE6 breaking teal dots, appears at the left edge. An off-white question card appears at the top: 'Nitric oxide stops: what lowers cGMP?'
scenes.narration: But nitric oxide does not last. Once it stops arriving, the cyclase falls quiet. Think back to the rod, where an enzyme destroyed this same messenger. What could bring cGMP back down, so the muscle tightens again?

scenes.visual: Hold the question card 'Nitric oxide stops: what lowers cGMP?' clearly visible for 4.5 seconds. The teal gauge trembles gently at its high level beneath a pulsing question mark, and the dimmed rose PDE5 in the corner stays unlabelled so the answer is not given away.

scenes.caption: A phosphodiesterase, just as in the rod. Here it is called PDE5, and it breaks cGMP into inactive GMP. Relaxation lasts only while synthesis keeps up with this breakdown. When synthesis stops, the muscle tightens again.
scenes.tts: A phosphodiesterase, just as in the rod. Here it is called P D E five, and it breaks c G M P into inactive G M P. Relaxation lasts only while synthesis keeps up with this breakdown. When synthesis stops, the muscle tightens again.
scenes.visual: The question card and rod inset clear. Rose (#F43F5E) PDE5 brightens and gains its label 'PDE5', converting teal (#2DD4BF) cGMP dots into fading grey GMP dots. The teal gauge falls back toward a dashed baseline, the contractile filaments shorten again, and the lumen narrows to its resting width.
scenes.narration: A phosphodiesterase, just as in the rod. Here it is called PDE5, and it breaks cGMP into inactive GMP. Relaxation lasts only while synthesis keeps up with this breakdown. When synthesis stops, the muscle tightens again.

scenes.tts: Two familiar drugs act on opposite sides of this balance. Nitroglycerin, given for chest pain since the nineteenth century, is converted in tissue into nitric oxide. It drives synthesis up even without endothelial signals. Sildenafil sits inside the catalytic pocket of P D E five. By slowing hydrolysis, it lets each burst of the messenger last longer.

scenes.visual: On the same smooth muscle cell, show two clean drug icons entering from opposite sides: on the left, 'Nitroglycerin' releases a bright plume of violet (#C084FC) nitric oxide directly onto emerald-green soluble guanylyl cyclase; on the right, a crisp white wedge labelled 'Sildenafil' slides squarely into the pocket of rose (#F43F5E) PDE5, slowing teal cGMP removal (schematic).

scenes.tts: Now place the rod from the first film beside this smooth muscle cell. Both use teal c G M P and a rose phosphodiesterase, yet wiring reverses the enzyme's role. In the rod, its breakdown enzyme creates the light signal. In the artery, breakdown ends relaxation.

scenes.visual: Split the frame smoothly: on the left, the first film's rod cell with teal cGMP falling and rose (#F43F5E) 'PDE6 makes the signal'; on the right, the smooth muscle cell with teal cGMP rising and rose (#F43F5E) 'PDE5 ends the signal'. Both sides stay cleanly animated with drifting teal dots moving in opposite directions.
scenes.narration: Now place the rod from the first film beside this smooth muscle cell. Both use teal cGMP and a rose phosphodiesterase, yet wiring reverses the enzyme's role. In the rod, its breakdown enzyme creates the light signal. In the artery, breakdown ends relaxation.

scenes.tts: Because arteries signal by raising c G M P, slowing breakdown strengthens the response to every burst of nitric oxide. Same molecule, opposite direction, different meaning. Keep this rule alongside the first. When rising c G M P carries the signal, blocking breakdown amplifies it.
